lessons.title: Sovereign Spreads and CDS: How the Market Prices Country Risk in Real Time

children.text: The last lesson ended on a limitation: rating agencies move in committee cycles, sometimes taking months to react to a deteriorating credit story. The bond and derivatives markets do not wait for a committee. Every single trading day, sovereign bond spreads and credit default swaps put a live, continuously updating price on how risky a country's debt is, and they very often move well before any agency picks up the phone.
Sovereign Bond Spreads: The Market's Running Commentary

markDefs.definition: The difference between the yield on a country's foreign-currency bond and the yield on a risk-free benchmark of the same maturity, usually a US Treasury bond, expressed in basis points. One basis point equals 0.01 percentage point.

children.text: is the extra yield investors demand to hold a country's dollar bond over a US Treasury bond of the same maturity, treated as the closest thing global markets have to a risk-free rate. If a country's 10-year dollar bond yields 8.5% while the 10-year US Treasury yields 4.2%, the spread is 430 basis points. That spread is compensation for exactly the country risk this chapter has been building up: economic, political, and currency risk, all rolled into one continuously traded number. The standard benchmark for tracking this across emerging markets is JPMorgan's EMBI (Emerging Markets Bond Index), whose spread level is quoted constantly across financial media as shorthand for how nervous or comfortable the market currently is about EM credit risk as a whole.

body.text: India does not issue sovereign dollar bonds, as covered in Chapter 1, so there is no direct India sovereign spread to quote the way there is for, say, Brazil or Indonesia. Analysts instead watch two proxies: the spread on dollar bonds issued by large Indian quasi-sovereign borrowers, like SBI, EXIM Bank of India, or ONGC, over Treasuries, and India's own sovereign CDS, which trades even without a cash bond behind it, covered next.

children.text: Credit Default Swaps: Insurance on a Government's Promise

markDefs.definition: A derivative contract in which the buyer makes periodic payments to the seller in exchange for a payout if a specified 'credit event', typically a default or a debt restructuring, occurs on a reference borrower's debt. Originally designed as insurance, it is now also traded purely as a bet on a borrower's creditworthiness.

children.text: works like insurance on a bond, even a sovereign bond. The buyer pays an annual premium, quoted in basis points of the notional amount insured, and the seller agrees to pay out if the referenced government defaults or restructures its debt. A country's 5-year CDS spread is one of the purest, most liquid, real-time readings of market-implied default risk available, and unlike a cash bond spread, it can be quoted on a sovereign even when that sovereign has issued little or no foreign-currency debt itself, since the contract references the country's broader foreign-currency obligations, not one specific bond.

body.caption: A simplified approximation of the market-implied annual probability of default from a CDS spread. Real-world pricing models are more layered, factoring in survival probabilities across multiple years, but this single-period approximation is a useful starting intuition.

children.text: Work through it with round numbers. If a country's 5-year CDS trades at a spread of 300 basis points (3.00%) and the market assumes a typical sovereign recovery rate of 40% (meaning bondholders expect to recover 40 paise on the rupee, or 40 cents on the dollar, in a restructuring), the market-implied annual default probability is roughly 3% divided by (1 minus 0.40), which works out to about 5%. That is not a certainty, it is the market's rough, continuously updated best guess, and it moves the moment new information arrives, long before any rating agency committee convenes.

body.title: Calculate the Implied Default Probability
body.prompt: A country's 5-year sovereign CDS trades at a spread of 500 basis points (5.00%). The market assumes a recovery rate of 25% in the event of default. Using the simplified approximation from this lesson, what is the market-implied annual probability of default, in percent?
body.explanation: Using PD is approximately equal to the CDS spread divided by (1 minus the recovery rate): 5% divided by (1 minus 0.25), which is 5% divided by 0.75, equals approximately 6.67%. A lower assumed recovery rate pushes the implied default probability higher for the same spread, since the market is pricing in a bigger loss if a default actually occurs.

children.text: Ratings vs Spreads and CDS: Which Moves First?

body.caption: Two Different Ways the Market Reads Country Risk

cells: Periodic; reviewed on a schedule, changed after committee deliberation
Continuous; repriced every time the market trades
A structured, methodology-driven opinion across five broad factors
Real-time investor sentiment and immediate news flow
Can lag actual deterioration by months, sometimes longer
Often the earliest visible warning sign, moving well ahead of a downgrade
Institutional mandates, index inclusion rules, regulatory capital frameworks
Traders, portfolio managers adjusting exposure day to day

children.text: Sri Lanka's own 2022 default is the textbook illustration of this lag. Sri Lanka's dollar bond yields and CDS spreads began widening sharply through 2021, well before its formal default and before the rating agencies had finished cutting it all the way to default-grade territory. Investors trading the bonds and the CDS were reacting to falling forex reserves and mounting external payment pressure in close to real time. The agencies eventually caught up, but by the time the formal downgrades to D (default) landed, the market had already been pricing severe distress for months. The next chapter walks through exactly this case in full.

body.title: Reading the Market Before the Rating
body.scenario: A country is currently rated BB (stable outlook) by all three major agencies. Over the past three months, its 5-year CDS spread has widened from 250 basis points to 900 basis points, and its dollar bond yields have risen sharply, even though no rating agency has changed its rating or outlook yet.
body.prompt: As an analyst, how would you interpret this gap between the unchanged rating and the sharply widening spreads, and what would you do with that information?
body.modelAnswer: The market is telling you something the rating has not yet caught up to. A near four-fold widening in CDS spreads over three months signals that traders and bondholders believe default or restructuring risk has risen sharply, likely due to specific news, such as falling reserves, political instability, or a stalled reform programme, that has not yet worked its way through a full rating committee review. A careful analyst would treat this widening as an early warning sign, investigate the underlying cause directly rather than waiting for the rating agencies, and expect a rating downgrade or a negative outlook change to likely follow if the underlying pressure does not ease.

body.title: Quick Check
body.question: Why can a country's 5-year CDS be actively traded even if that country has never issued a dollar-denominated sovereign bond, like India?
options: CDS contracts can only be written on corporate debt, not sovereign debt, so this scenario is not actually possible
The CDS references the sovereign's broader foreign-currency payment obligations as a whole, not one specific bond, so it can be quoted independent of whether a dollar bond exists
The CDS instead references the country's local-currency government bonds only
Such a CDS would have no meaningful market price and would not actually trade
body.explanation: A sovereign CDS contract is written against a sovereign's foreign-currency payment obligations broadly, using a defined basket of eligible reference obligations, rather than against one single bond. That is exactly why India's CDS can trade and provide a real-time read on market-implied country risk even though the Indian government itself has never issued a dollar bond, as covered in Chapter 1.

body.text: A credit rating is the market's yearbook photo, taken periodically, carefully composed, and quickly out of date. Bond spreads and CDS are the live security camera feed, noisier, but almost always the first place a real problem shows up.

children.text: This closes out the country risk framework: the three pillars, how agencies formalise them into a rating, India's own rating journey, and how the market continuously reprices all of it through spreads and CDS. The next chapter turns to what happens when all of this goes wrong at once, starting with the warning signs of a sovereign debt crisis and a full walkthrough of Sri Lanka's 2022 default.

points: A sovereign spread is the extra yield investors demand over a risk-free benchmark, usually US Treasuries, to compensate for a country's economic, political, and currency risk.
India has no direct sovereign dollar bond spread since it does not issue dollar sovereign bonds; analysts instead watch quasi-sovereign dollar bond spreads and India's own sovereign CDS.

A sovereign CDS is default insurance on a government's foreign-currency obligations, and its spread gives a simplified, market-implied annual default probability of roughly spread divided by (1 minus the assumed recovery rate).
Spreads and CDS are continuously repriced and often move well ahead of formal rating actions, making them a useful early warning signal, as Sri Lanka's 2021-22 experience showed.
Ratings and market-based pricing serve different users and update on different timelines. A careful analyst reads both rather than relying on either alone.

body.text: The spread levels, CDS pricing, and numerical examples in this lesson are illustrative and simplified for teaching purposes, not live market quotes or precise pricing models. Check a live data source such as Bloomberg, a broker terminal, or JPMorgan's published EMBI data for current spread and CDS levels before using them in analysis or advice.
